Seeding the Database from TheCocktailDB - Part 2 # Link to the external API: TheCocktailDB.
This is the second part of my documentation for the process of seeding my database with data from TheCocktailDB API. In my last entry, I covered the overall pipeline, some of the problems with the API and its data compared to my model, the classes CocktailDBFetcher and IngredientAnalyser, and why I chose this procedure instead of other alternatives.
In this part I will cover the classification files, the importer, and the bugs I ran into along the way.
Stage 3: The classification files # This is the heart of the design, and the part where the reasoning is easiest to forget. It took me some time to get to this process, and I had to lean on the help of an AI to get through this point. I will therefore explain it in detail, and point out the places where the AI did the majority of the work.
For the classification, I have two files, not one:
ingredient-aliases.csv (raw name → canonical name) # // An example of a few rows in the file raw,canonical light rum,White Rum kahlua,Coffee Liqueur absolut vodka,Vodka fresh lime juice,Lime Juice // .... This file answers the question: “The API wrote this. So what do I call it?” It maps many raw names to one canonical name, so I do not end up with three different ways to write “Lime Juice”. The file has 293 rows, one per distinct raw name.
canonical-ingredients.csv (canonical name → type and intensities) # // An example of a few rows in the file canonical,type,sweet,sour,bitter,salty,spicy White Rum,SPIRIT,2,1,1,1,1 Coffee Liqueur,LIQUEUR,4,1,3,1,1 Lime Juice,MIXER,1,5,1,1,1 Lime,GARNISH,,,,, Ice,IGNORE,,,,, // .... This file answers: “What is this ingredient in my model?” It has 132 rows, where each canonical ingredient has a type (SPIRIT, LIQUEUR, MIXER, SYRUP, GARNISH or IGNORE) and, for the four types that carry flavor, five intensities from 1 to 5.
Why two files instead of one # The answer is that the relationship is many-to-one. Kahlua, Tia Maria and coffee brandy are three different names for roughly one thing in my model. If I had put the intensities on the raw names, I would have repeated the same five numbers many times and risked them drifting apart when I changed one. With two files, I make sure that each flavor value is stored once, on the canonical ingredient, and the aliases file only handles naming. This is the same idea as database normalization, just applied to the seed data on a file level.
It is also important to note that this is just my way of doing it. I could have chosen to value each raw-named ingredient as its own “entity”. After all, some brands of gin taste sweeter and some more bitter than others, and you could therefore argue that treating them as roughly one thing is not true to reality. However, I chose this restriction of my model to keep a tighter and more manageable scope for myself. After all, this is “only” an educational project.
The special values # IGNORE marks ingredients that should not affect the model at all: ice, water, egg white, salt, bitters and similar. They do not change which spirit or mixer a drink is built on. GARNISH ingredients become the optional garnish. They have no intensities because garnish has no flavor profile in my schema. UNCLASSIFIED appears only in the aliases file, for the 30 names that were deliberately left unclassified (for example advocaat and cream of coconut). A drink that uses one of these is skipped. An honest limitation: the files and intensities are AI-generated # As I stated earlier, I received help from an AI assistant for some of this process. The biggest part was the creation of the two classification files. To save time and avoid unnecessary effort and hours, I chose to let an AI make them for me at my request. I of course told it how to categorize the ingredients and how the files should classify the data, but I did not write the files myself. I did, however, review the result, but overall I chose to stick with what the AI wrote for now.
The intensity numbers (sweet, sour, bitter, salty, spicy, 1 to 5) were also produced by an AI assistant at my request, based on general knowledge of how these ingredients usually taste. They are not measured data, they were not taken from a taste database, and they are not the result of a taste test. They are therefore subjective and probably not entirely right: one person may find gin more bitter than the file says, another may find a liqueur less sweet.
That is acceptable for this application, given the circumstances: after all, this is only an educational project. However, it must be stated clearly that the quiz is not scientifically accurate because of these estimates. It ranks cocktails relative to each other, so what matters most is that the numbers are consistent (sweet liqueurs score higher on sweet than dry spirits) and not that each individual number is perfect. And because all intensities live in one file, canonical-ingredients.csv, they can be corrected in one place without changing any code.
One thing to be aware of is that many of the choices in the alias file are rough simplifications. When a raw name had no exact match among my canonical ingredients, it was mapped to the closest one, even though they do not taste the same. For example, aperol is mapped to Campari, although Aperol is noticeably sweeter and less bitter, and mezcal is mapped to Tequila, which ignores its smoky character. In the same way, pomegranate juice becomes Cranberry Juice, strawberry schnapps becomes Peach Schnapps and coconut milk becomes Cream.
Each of these mappings is a trade-off between keeping the list of canonical ingredients short and keeping each ingredient true to reality. I chose a short list to keep the scope manageable, but it means that some drinks will have a flavor profile that is slightly different from how the real drink tastes. Because the mappings live in one file, they can be refined later by adding a new canonical ingredient and pointing the alias to it.
Stage 4: The import (CocktailImporter) # CocktailImporter reads the raw JSON and both CSV files, and for each drink decides: save it, or skip it and say why.
Step by step for one drink # Go through strIngredient1 to strIngredient15. Ignore empty ones. Add each ingredient and its measure to a text list (this ends up in the cocktail’s description, because my schema has no separate measure columns). Normalize the name, look it up in the aliases file, then look up the canonical entry. If either lookup fails or the alias is UNCLASSIFIED, skip the drink with reason UNCLASSIFIED_INGREDIENT. Depending on the type: IGNORE: do nothing. GARNISH: remember just the first one (because my model only allows one garnish per drink). anything else: remember it for that type. If the drink already has a different ingredient of the same type, skip it with reason TOO_MANY_OF_TYPE. If the drink has no spirit, liqueur, mixer or syrup after this, skip it with reason NO_INGREDIENTS_AFTER_IGNORE. Otherwise, find or create the family, spirit, liqueur, mixer, syrup and garnish, create the cocktail, and save it. The code that enforces the one-per-type rule is this switch:
private Optional<String> classifyAndSave(EntityManager em, JsonNode drink, String name) { // Variables and additional code switch (c.type()) { case "IGNORE" -> { } // ice, water, bitters ... case "GARNISH" -> { if (garnish == null) garnish = c.name(); } // keep the first garnish default -> { String existing = byType.putIfAbsent(c.type(), c.name()); // type -> ingredient if (existing != null && !existing.equals(c.name())) { return skip(name, "TOO_MANY_OF_TYPE", c.type() + ": " + existing + " + " + c.name()); } } } // Building Cocktail and catching exceptions } byType is a Map<String, String> from type to ingredient (for example SPIRIT -> Vodka). putIfAbsent stores the ingredient if the type is free, and returns the existing one if the type is already taken. A second, different ingredient of the same type means the drink does not fit.
One subtle rule: the same canonical ingredient appearing twice is not “too many”. Sugar and Powdered sugar both become Sugar, so that is fine. Only two different ingredients of the same type break the model.
Why drinks are skipped instead of forced to fit # At the start of this project, when I built my model, it did not occur to me that some recipes would have more than one ingredient of the same type. To incorporate this now, it would be necessary to revisit my model and maybe even reorganize it completely. My model only allows one spirit, one liqueur, one mixer and one syrup per cocktail. Many real cocktails have two or more spirits (for example a Long Island Iced Tea). I could have picked one arbitrarily, but then the stored recipe would be wrong, and the flavor profile would be wrong with it. I preferred a smaller, correct data set over a larger, distorted one. This was a conscious trade-off, and it matches the decision to skip non-fitting recipes rather than remodel the schema (which would have grown the scope).
Skipped drinks are data, not errors # A skipped drink is an expected outcome, not something that went wrong, so it is not an exception. Each skip is recorded as a small object (name, reason, detail) and the whole list is written to database/seed/skipped-cocktails.json at the end. Real errors (a file that cannot be read, a database failure) are exceptions. This keeps the two situations separate: the first is part of the normal result, the second is a failure.
The skipped drinks are stored like this:
[{ "name" : "AT&T", "reason" : "TOO_MANY_OF_TYPE", "detail" : "SPIRIT: Vodka + Gin" }, { "name" : "Dirty Martini", "reason" : "UNCLASSIFIED_INGREDIENT", "detail" : "Olive Brine" }, { "name" : "Pineapple Gingerale Smoothie", "reason" : "NO_INGREDIENTS_AFTER_IGNORE", "detail" : "" }] This is how many drinks fall under each skip reason:
3 "reason" : "NO_INGREDIENTS_AFTER_IGNORE" 177 "reason" : "TOO_MANY_OF_TYPE" 24 "reason" : "UNCLASSIFIED_INGREDIENT" Find-or-create # Ingredient names are UNIQUE in the database, and the same ingredient is used by many cocktails. So for every spirit, liqueur, mixer, syrup, garnish, family and flavor tag, the importer first looks up by name and only creates the row if it does not exist. When it creates a spirit, liqueur, mixer or syrup, it also attaches the five flavor tags with the intensities from the canonical file. The FlavorTag rows (Sweet, Sour, Bitter, Salty, Spicy) are created the same way, the first time they are needed.
The generic helper that does this for every entity type:
private <T> T findOrCreate(EntityManager em, Class<T> type, String name, Supplier<T> creator) { List<T> found = em.createQuery( "SELECT e FROM " + type.getSimpleName() + " e WHERE e.name = :n", type) .setParameter("n", name).getResultList(); if (!found.isEmpty()) return found.get(0); // already in the database: reuse it T created = creator.get(); // otherwise build a new one ... em.persist(created); // ... and save it return created; } and a typical call, which creates a spirit with its flavor tags only if it does not exist yet:
if (byType.containsKey("SPIRIT")) cocktail.setSpirit(findOrCreate(em, Spirit.class, byType.get("SPIRIT"), () -> withTags(new Spirit(byType.get("SPIRIT"), null), em, "SPIRIT"))); The tag names are the English column names from the CSV, and the frontend can translate them to Danish later on. That way, the database holds stable identifiers and changing a display word never requires a data change.
One transaction per drink # Each drink is saved in its own transaction. If one drink fails, the drinks before it stay saved, and only that drink is rolled back. This also means the importer can be rerun safely.
Rerunning (idempotence) # Before saving, the importer checks whether a cocktail with that name already exists. If it does, it is counted as “already existed” and left untouched. The consequence is important: if I change the classification files, I must reset the database before importing again, otherwise the old rows remain. I learned this the hard way (described in more detail later in this entry).
Families # I did not have my own cocktail families yet, so the family name comes from TheCocktailDB’s strCategory (for example Cocktail, Shot, Ordinary Drink). Drinks marked Non alcoholic go into a family called Mocktails. Families are created through find-or-create, so I can rename or merge them in the database later without touching the importer.
Why the importer uses the EntityManager directly instead of my DAOs # My DAOs open a short-lived EntityManager for each operation. The importer needs one EntityManager shared across the whole run, so that a spirit created for drink 1 is a managed object that drink 2 can reuse, and so it can control one transaction per drink. It also does not go through CocktailService, because that service checks things like “is the caller an admin” and validates ids, which makes sense for an HTTP request but not for a trusted offline tool.
The trade-off is real and I want to be honest about it: the importer bypasses the DAO and service layers and duplicates the rule “a cocktail needs at least one ingredient”. I accept that because the seed is a one-off tool that lives in its own package (app.seed) and is not part of the running API.
What went wrong along the way (and what it taught me) # These are worth including because each one shows how I went about debugging my code.
Problem Cause Lesson skipped-cocktails.json stayed empty although 204 drinks were skipped My run() method was missing the call to writeSkipped() and the final log line. The log showed no Import done line, which was the clue. Read the log for what is missing, not only for errors. Mocktails ended up in the wrong family A typo: the code compared with "Non alcoholics", but the API says "Non alcoholic". Existing rows are never updated, so after fixing the code I had to reset the database. The importer said 222 already existed after I reran schema.sql The IntelliJ data source pointed at a different database (postgres) than the application used. Always check which database a script runs against. wrong column type [intensity] ... found SMALLINT, expecting INTEGER The schema used SMALLINT, but the entity field is a Java int. This is exactly what hbm2ddl.auto=validate is for: it catches schema/entity mismatches early. I changed the schema to INTEGER. new Garnish(name, null) did not compile Garnish used @AllArgsConstructor, which includes the id. Lombok-generated constructors depend on the field list; I removed @AllArgsConstructor from Garnish and used the no-arg constructor and setters instead. Limitations and what I would do differently # About 48% of the fetched drinks (204 of 426) were skipped because they have more than one ingredient of the same type, or an ingredient I did not classify. The data model is simpler than reality, and I chose to keep it that way for a more manageable scope. The intensities are AI-generated, subjective estimates. If I had more time, I would choose to set the flavor intensities myself or, even better, run some sort of survey to gather results as close to reality as possible. Only the first garnish is kept, and measures live as plain text in description, so the app cannot scale a recipe or search by quantity. File paths are relative (database/seed/...), so the importer must be run from the project root. No incremental update. Changing a classification means resetting the database. A more advanced importer would be able to update existing rows, and this would also be more desirable if the app were ever to go into production. Possible API limit of 25 drinks per letter. Data source terms. The free TheCocktailDB key is meant for development and learning. If the app were ever published commercially, the terms and attribution would need to be checked. If I had more time, I would add more aliases to reduce skips, support a second spirit per cocktail, and turn the importer into a repeatable command with a “reset and seed” option.

Seeding the Database from TheCocktailDB - Part 1 # Link to the external API: TheCocktailDB.
This post documents how the database was filled with real cocktail recipes: where the data comes from, how it is transformed to fit my data model, and why the process is built the way it is. It is the part of the project that took the most effort to get right, so I will describe the decisions in detail, including the alternatives I rejected and the bugs I hit.
I chose to tackle this part of the project as late as I did because I believed it was important to ensure that my database, entities, DAO layer and most of the service layer were in place before I started the data seeding. I stand by this decision, but looking back I should have examined the data more before building so much of the project architecture. I believe that would have saved me from many of the problems I encountered, for example the fact that 204 of the fetched drinks were rejected, many of them because they had more than one ingredient of the same type. So this is a lesson I will take with me in the future.
Because this part is as complicated and big as it is, I have chosen to split the documentation up into two parts, to avoid having one huge entry.
The problem # My application recommends a cocktail based on a quiz of sorts. To do that, the database needs more than just a recipe name. Every cocktail points to one spirit, liqueur, mixer and syrup (all optional) and an optional garnish. Every spirit, liqueur, mixer and syrup carries flavor intensities from 1 to 5 for five dimensions: sweet, sour, bitter, salty and spicy. The quiz sums these intensities per cocktail and compares the result with what the user answered. As I have covered multiple times throughout this series, this is the core idea of my project. It is what distinguishes this project from so many other drink recipe applications.
TheCocktailDB is a free public API with 637 recipes (as stated on their website), which is why I chose this API in the first place. After all, it should be perfect for my project, and it mostly is, but its data does not fit my model in three major ways:
Free-text ingredients. A drink has up to 15 ingredient fields (strIngredient1 … strIngredient15) with free text such as Light rum, Bacardi Limon, Kahlua and Fresh lime juice. The same kind of ingredient appears under many different names. No categories. The API does not say whether an ingredient is a spirit, a liqueur, a mixer or a syrup. My schema needs exactly that. Of course this is a structural choice I made, and I knew from the start that the API would not necessarily have these categories, so I was prepared for this. No flavor data at all. Intensities do not exist in the API. They had to be added by me (with help from an AI assistant, see Part 2). This was another problem I knew I would have to tackle. So seeding was not a simple copy, unfortunately. It is a transformation from the API’s loose data into my strict relational model. The rest of this post is about how that transformation was made possible.
Alternatives I considered # Approach Why I did not choose it Call the API live when the app runs The app would depend on an external service being up and fast. The quiz needs flavor profiles, which the API does not have, so I would still need my own data. The queries in the quiz (filter by family and spirit, then score) are also much easier against my own tables than against an API. Write all recipes by hand as an SQL script Full control, but far too slow for hundreds of recipes. It would also hide how the data was produced, which is not ideal for documentation. Import everything first, then assign intensities afterwards This was my first idea, and what I thought I was going to do. The problem with this method is that I would import drinks that break my one-ingredient-per-type rule, and then have to repair them manually in the database. I preferred to decide the rules before importing so the database never contains data that violates my model. Of course I could have made the rules fit the data better, but then I would have been forced to change a lot of the structure I had already built. What I chose # Approach Pros and cons Fetch once, classify with my own files, then import with a Java program This way was heavier and required many extra steps to transform the data, unfortunately. However, the positive side of this process is that it is repeatable, and every step can be inspected: the raw JSON is on disk, the classification is in readable CSV files, and rejected drinks are written to a file instead of disappearing. I can easily go through the rejected data and make the necessary changes to the system so that it can incorporate the rejected data later. The key idea in the chosen approach is that the seed is a one-time offline process, not a runtime feature. The finished application only ever talks to its own database. If the data in TheCocktailDB changes, it has no effect on my database, and if I (as admin) need to add or change data, I can do that without major consequences for the seeded data. This holds as long as I do not rerun schema.sql, because that would delete all data from the database, but that is a whole other problem in itself.
The pipeline at a glance # TheCocktailDB API | | (1) CocktailDBFetcher - 26 HTTP requests, in parallel (threads) | v database/seed/raw/a.json ... z.json <- raw cache, never edited by hand | | (2) IngredientAnalyser - counts every distinct ingredient name | v database/seed/ingredient-candidates.csv <- 293 distinct names | | (3) Classify them into two CSV files (drafted with AI assistance and reviewed by me) | v database/seed/ingredient-aliases.csv <- raw name -> canonical name database/seed/canonical-ingredients.csv <- canonical name -> type + 5 intensities | | (4) CocktailImporter - applies the rules, writes to PostgreSQL | v PostgreSQL (222 cocktails) and database/seed/skipped-cocktails.json (204 drinks) Each stage saves its result as a file on disk, and the next stage starts by reading that file. The alternative would be to keep everything in memory and pass Java objects from one stage to the next, but then the data would be lost every time the program stops. That is deliberate. Because the files stay on disk, I can rerun stage 4 as many times as I like without calling the API again, and if something goes wrong I can open the file between two stages and see exactly what went in.
All files live under database/seed/, next to schema.sql, because they are data and not source code. The Java classes live in the package app.seed.
Stage 1: Fetching the data (CocktailDBFetcher) # What it does # TheCocktailDB does not have an endpoint that returns all drinks at once, so my first challenge was to import as many cocktails as possible using the other endpoints available. The one I found most useful was searching by first letter (search.php?f=a). The fetcher requests all 26 letters and saves each response unchanged as raw JSON in database/seed/raw/<letter>.json.
Why by letter # I needed a way to get all recipes, not one by name. The letter endpoint returns the full recipe (ingredients, measures, instructions, category) in one call, so 26 requests were meant to cover the whole database. The alternative (listing by category and then looking up every drink by id) would need hundreds of requests, but I was prepared to use that method if searching by letter did not work.
Why threads # In this third semester we have learned a lot of new, useful techniques and tools for developing our API, and one of them is concurrency (threading). I therefore strive to incorporate each tool at least once, where it makes sense, and this is a place where threads make real sense. Each request spends almost all of its time waiting for the network, not computing, so running several at once speeds up the process considerably.
The implementation uses:
HttpClient from the Java standard library, so no extra dependency an ExecutorService with a fixed pool of 4 threads one task per letter, which returns a Future, and the main thread collects the results The core of it looks like this:
// Inside fetchAll() ExecutorService executor = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(THREAD_COUNT); try { List<Future<String>> futures = new ArrayList<>(); for (char letter = 'a'; letter <= 'z'; letter++) { final char current = letter; futures.add(executor.submit(() -> fetchLetter(current))); } for (Future<String> future : futures) { try { logger.info(future.get()); } catch (ExecutionException e) { logger.error("Fetch failed: {}", e.getCause().getMessage(), e.getCause()); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); logger.error("Fetching was interrupted"); return; } } } finally { executor.shutdown(); } // The rest of the code A Future is a receipt for work that is running on another thread and may not be finished yet. executor.submit(...) returns it immediately, and future.get() waits until the task is done and gives me its result, or throws an ExecutionException if the task failed.
Why a Future and not a plain Thread? A Thread runs a Runnable, and run() returns void, so it cannot hand back a result, and an exception inside it disappears into that thread instead of reaching the code that started it. With a Future I get both the result (here a status line such as m: 25 drinks saved) and the failure, and an error for one letter does not stop the other 25. Other options exist, such as CompletableFuture or parallel streams, but they are more advanced, and parallel streams do not let me choose the number of threads, which I wanted for a public API. ExecutorService with Future is the most direct way to say “do these independent jobs in parallel, then collect the answers”.
I chose 4 threads because it is enough to give a clear speedup while staying polite to a free public API. Firing 26 requests at once would be a bit over the top and not necessary at all.
Why not threads in the database layer # I also considered using threads when saving to the database, and decided against it. A JPA EntityManager is not thread-safe; sharing one between threads gives unpredictable errors. Each thread would need its own EntityManager and transaction, and the unique names (a spirit that appears in many drinks) would cause races between threads that both try to create the same row. The network part is slow and independent, so it benefits from threads. The database part is fast and has shared state, so it does not. The import takes about three seconds single-threaded, so there was nothing to gain.
Caching and repeatability # If a letter’s file already exists, the fetcher skips it. It writes a file only after the response has been parsed successfully, so a broken or half-finished response never ends up in the cache. That makes the fetch safe to rerun after a failure, and it means I normally fetch only once.
Result # The fetch returned 426 drinks in total. Letters u and x returned nothing. Nine letters returned exactly 25 drinks, which indicates a cap on the API’s side. However, this is not something I know for sure. It is only interesting to note that the letters that returned 25 drinks did so every time I fetched from the API, and no letter ever returned more than 25 drinks. The API says it holds 637 drinks in total, but only 426 drinks were fetched, so a lot of the recipes never reach my program. This is of course something to look into later, if time allows.
Stage 2: Finding out what the data contains (IngredientAnalyser) # Before I could decide how to classify the ingredients, I needed to know what was there. IngredientAnalyser reads all the raw JSON files, normalizes every ingredient name (trim, lowercase, collapse repeated spaces) and counts how often each one occurs. The result is written to ingredient-candidates.csv.
The core of the counting is these few lines:
String name = normalize(node.asText()); // " Light Rum " -> "light rum" if (!name.isEmpty()) { counts.merge(name, 1, Integer::sum); // first time: 1, afterwards: +1 } The output file has two columns, ingredient,count, sorted with the most common ingredient first.
The result was 293 distinct ingredient names across the 426 drinks. The number of ingredient usages is the sum of the count column in ingredient-candidates.csv, which is 1,672 (each time a drink mentions an ingredient, it counts once). Without normalization, Vodka, vodka and Vodka would have counted as three different ingredients.
The reason this step exists is that it turns a vague task (“classify the ingredients”) into a finite, measurable one (“classify these 293 names, starting with the most frequent”). Because the file is sorted by count, the most common ingredients come first, so I could get good coverage with limited effort. That matters because I have limited time on this project.
More information in the next entry # That was it for this part of the seeding of my database. I will continue the documentation and explanation in the next entry.

The course requires three kinds of tests: unit tests, integration tests and REST-assured tests. They answer different questions and can be written at different points in the project. This part documents the unit and integration tests written so far, the infrastructure behind them, the mistakes I made along the way, and what the tests deliberately do not cover.
Testing strategy: test what is different, not what is identical # All 14 DAOs inherit the same CRUD methods from AbstractDAO. Writing one test class per DAO would test the same code 14 times. Instead I tested AbstractDAO’s CRUD once, through UserDAO, and only wrote targeted tests for classes where the behavior differs. I mainly focused on the places where the code is most critical and errors are most likely. My main focus was anything that touched my database. After all, the next step after testing was to seed the database with data from the external API, so I had to make sure that all CRUD methods and specialized queries worked before that.
Critical classes that also needed testing # CocktailDAO: five nullable relations, a shared JOIN FETCH query, and the quiz candidate query. CocktailMenuDAO: a composite key mapped with @EmbeddedId and @MapsId, which is a different mapping pattern from the simple entities. Spirit: cascading of flavor tags through a join entity (covered inside the CocktailDAO flavor-profile test). Simple entities such as Garnish and CocktailFamily contain nothing but plain columns, so they carry little risk and are exercised indirectly as test data in the other tests. They needed no special attention, so I skipped over them fairly quickly.
Unit tests # Unit tests exercise one class in isolation, with no database. EuclideanDistanceStrategy is a good fit because it is pure math and holds the whole matching logic. It is critical that this class calculates the correct distance, which makes it the obvious choice:
public class EuclideanDistanceStrategyTest { private final EuclideanDistanceStrategy strategy = new EuclideanDistanceStrategy(); @Test void identicalProfilesHaveZeroDistance() { Map<Long, Integer> profile = Map.of(1L, 5, 2L, 3); assertEquals(0.0, strategy.calculateDistance(profile, profile), 0.0001); // delta parameter needed because double-calculations can have microscopic differences in result } @Test void calculateKnownDistanceCorrectly() { Map<Long, Integer> userAnswers = Map.of(1L, 5, 2L, 1); Map<Long, Integer> cocktailProfile = Map.of(1L, 3, 2L, 1); // Difference: dim1 = 5-3=2, dim2 = 1-1=0 → √(2² + 0²) = √4 = 2.0 assertEquals(2.0, strategy.calculateDistance(userAnswers, cocktailProfile), 0.0001); } @Test // Most important test - tests that a NullPointerException is not thrown if some dimensions are missing void missingDimensionCountsAsZero() { Map<Long, Integer> userAnswers = Map.of(1L, 5); Map<Long, Integer> cocktailProfile = Map.of(2L, 5); // dim1: 5-0=5, dim2: 0-5=-5 → √(25+25) = √50 ≈ 7.0711 assertEquals(Math.sqrt(50), strategy.calculateDistance(userAnswers, cocktailProfile), 0.0001); } } The three tests increase in difficulty:
The first test is the simplest case: identical input gives 0. I compare profile to profile to simulate a user answer and a candidate with identical values. Two identical flavor profiles are a perfect match, and I wanted to make sure that a perfect match gives a distance of 0 as expected. assertEquals needs a delta (0.0001) because floating-point arithmetic can produce tiny rounding errors, so an exact comparison of two double values could fail even when the result is correct.
The second test uses a known distance that I calculated by hand and checks that the code reaches the same result. This shows that the logic is correct and that I can trust the calculation.
The last and most difficult test is an edge case that exercises the getOrDefault line. Without that line, a dimension missing from one of the maps would cause a NullPointerException. The user can choose not to rate every flavor dimension, so one or more dimensions might be missing. The test also covers a cocktail candidate that is missing dimensions. That will most likely not happen, because I have decided that all candidates will always have all five, but I wanted to be sure that the calculation would not fail if it did.
Integration test infrastructure # A real database in Docker # Integration tests run against a real PostgreSQL database started by Testcontainers. I chose it over mocks or an in-memory database because the JPA mappings are then tested against the same database engine as production. Of course, this means Docker must be running locally.
My project uses Testcontainers 2.x. The module is named testcontainers-postgresql, and the container class moved to a new package and is no longer generic:
import org.testcontainers.postgresql.PostgreSQLContainer; // Other imports public final class TestHibernateConfig { // Variables, constructor and getEntityManagerFactory() private static void startContainer() { container = new PostgreSQLContainer("postgres:16") .withDatabaseName("test_db") .withUsername("test") .withPassword("test"); container.start(); } private static Properties buildProps() { Properties props = HibernateBaseProperties.createBase(); props.put("hibernate.hbm2ddl.auto", "create-drop"); props.put("hibernate.connection.url", container.getJdbcUrl()); props.put("hibernate.connection.username", container.getUsername()); props.put("hibernate.connection.password", container.getPassword()); return props; } } The test configuration uses create-drop: Hibernate builds the schema from the entities for each test run. That is intentional, because the goal of these tests is to verify that entities and DAOs work together. Because of this, the ON DELETE CASCADE and ON DELETE SET NULL rules from my script do not exist in the test database, so I have deliberately not written a test that deletes a user and expects the favorite cocktails to disappear as well. Such a test would fail, not because of my code, but because the delete rules only exist in schema.sql and are not something Hibernate knows about. Whether the entities match schema.sql is verified separately with hbm2ddl.auto=validate (set in config.properties) against the real database, so it does not need an integration test.
Making the DAOs testable # The first version of AbstractDAO always fetched HibernateConfig.getEntityManagerFactory(), which meant any test would have hit my development database. The tests exposed this architectural gap. The fix was constructor injection of the EntityManagerFactory, so a test can pass in its own:
protected AbstractDAO(Class<T> entityClass) { this(entityClass, HibernateConfig.getEntityManagerFactory()); } protected AbstractDAO(Class<T> entityClass, EntityManagerFactory emf) { this.entityClass = entityClass; this.emf = emf; } The production code is unchanged (the simple constructor works as before), but integration tests can now inject their own EntityManagerFactory:
class UserDAOIntegrationTest extends IntegrationTestBase { private UserDAO userDAO; @BeforeEach void setup() { userDAO = new UserDAO(emf); } } A shared base class # All intergrationtest extends an abstract class called IntegrationTestBase. This abstract class holds a @BeforeAll method that creates an EntityManagerFactory and an @AfterEach method that cleans the database:
public abstract class IntegrationTestBase { protected static EntityManagerFactory emf; @BeforeAll static void initEmf() { emf = TestHibernateConfig.getEntityManagerFactory(); } @AfterEach void cleanDatabase() { try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) { em.getTransaction().begin(); // Deleted in order, so foreign keys do not block (children before parents) em.createQuery("DELETE FROM CocktailMenu").executeUpdate(); em.createQuery("DELETE FROM SpiritFlavorTag").executeUpdate(); // ... remaining join entities, then Cocktail, ingredients, family, FlavorTag, User em.getTransaction().commit(); } } } Rows are deleted children-first because foreign keys would otherwise block the deletes - the same reason schema.sql drops tables in a specific order.
Lesson learned: @AfterEach vs @AfterAll. My first run failed during test discovery because the cleanup method was annotated with @AfterAll. JUnit requires @AfterAll methods to be static, since they run once without a test instance. More importantly, @AfterAll would have been wrong even if made static: the database would only be cleaned once at the end, so data from one test would leak into the next and UNIQUE constraints would make later tests fail for reasons unrelated to the code. @AfterEach, on the other hand, guarantees that every test starts with an empty database, so data does not leak into later tests and UNIQUE constraints do not cause problems. @BeforeAll on the EntityManagerFactory setup is correct, though, and must be static, because I want to keep the same factory throughout the whole test class.
What the integration tests cover # UserDAOIntegrationTest: the shared CRUD logic # These tests establish that AbstractDAO’s transactions and mappings work. In UserDAOIntegrationTest, I test that it is possible to create a user, that I can retrieve the same user afterwards, and that deleting a user actually removes them from the database. I also test findByUsername(), both when the user exists and when they do not. In the latter case, the method has to return an empty Optional instead of throwing an exception, which it fortunately does. Writing them also showed me that my first version of the test class did not cover update at all, so I added a dedicated test for that later in the process:
@Test void updatePersistsChanges() { User saved = userDAO.create(new User("tempUser", "old@test.dk", "hashed_pw")); saved.setEmail("new@test.dk"); userDAO.update(saved); Optional<User> found = userDAO.getById(saved.getId()); assertTrue(found.isPresent()); assertEquals("new@test.dk", found.get().getEmail()); } This test matters because update uses em.merge(...). After create returns, the EntityManager that saved the user is closed, so the returned object is detached and Hibernate no longer tracks changes to it. Calling a setter alone changes nothing in the database. merge copies the changes into a new EntityManager, and reading the user back with a fresh getById proves the change was persisted.
CocktailDAOIntegrationTest: optional relations, JOIN FETCH and quiz candidates # The most important test recreates the Old Fashioned case: a cocktail saved with only a spirit, and no liqueur, mixer or syrup:
@Test // Test that cocktails without optional ingredients are still fetched by getByIdWithDetails() void cocktailNoOptionalIngredients() { CocktailFamily family = createFamily("Classics"); Spirit whiskey = createSpirit("Whiskey"); Cocktail saved = createCocktail("Old Fashioned", family, whiskey); Optional<Cocktail> found = cocktailDAO.getByIdWithDetails(saved.getId()); assertTrue(found.isPresent()); Cocktail cocktail = found.get(); // Works without exceptions because JOIN FETCH loaded the relations assertEquals("Whiskey", cocktail.getSpirit().getName()); assertEquals("Classics", cocktail.getCocktailFamily().getName()); assertNull(cocktail.getLiqueur()); assertNull(cocktail.getMixer()); assertNull(cocktail.getSyrup()); assertNull(cocktail.getGarnish()); } Calling getSpirit().getName() after the EntityManager has closed is itself the proof that JOIN FETCH worked.
A second test saves a mocktail without a spirit and checks that getAllWithDetails still returns it, which proves the query uses LEFT JOIN FETCH rather than a plain JOIN FETCH that would silently drop such cocktails:
A third test demonstrates the problem that JOIN FETCH solves, by deliberately triggering the exception with the plain getById:
@Test // Test that shows why using JOIN FETCH is necessary void plainGetByIdLeavesRelationsLazy() { CocktailFamily family = createFamily("Classics"); Cocktail saved = createCocktail("Old Fashioned", family, createSpirit("Whiskey")); Cocktail found = cocktailDAO.getById(saved.getId()).orElseThrow(); // EntityManager is closed, and spirit was never fetched assertThrows(LazyInitializationException.class, () -> found.getSpirit().getName()); } The remaining tests cover the quiz query. candidatesFilteredByFamily shows that the family filter is a hard filter: only cocktails from the chosen family are selected. spiritFilterIsOptional runs the same query twice, once with a spirit id (one cocktail remains) and once with null (both pass), which is exactly the “user has no spirit preference” case.
The flavor-profile test is the most demanding. It ensures that a cocktail’s flavor dimensions are calculated correctly. The test takes a cocktail with a spirit and a syrup that have different intensities per dimension, and checks that summing and ranking them gives the expected result. Salty and Spicy are given the same sum on purpose, so the tie-breaker case is tested too:
@Test // Checks that a candidate's flavor profile sums intensities and ranks dimensions void candidateFlavorProfile () { // Important - flavor tags need to be created in this order! FlavorTag sweet = flavorTagDAO.create(new FlavorTag("Sweet")); FlavorTag sour = flavorTagDAO.create(new FlavorTag("Sour")); FlavorTag bitter = flavorTagDAO.create(new FlavorTag("Bitter")); FlavorTag salty = flavorTagDAO.create(new FlavorTag("Salty")); FlavorTag spicy = flavorTagDAO.create(new FlavorTag("Spicy")); // Creates Spirit and Syrup, creates CocktailFamily and Cocktail, makes List<CocktailCandidates> /* Spirit: Sweet 1, Sour 2, Bitter 4, Salty 1, Spicy 1 Syrup: Sweet 5, Sour 1, Bitter 1, Salty 1, Spicy 1 Sums: Sweet 6, Sour 3, Bitter 5, Salty 2, Spicy 2 Ranking: Sweet 5, Bitter 4, Sour 3, Salty 2, Spicy 1 Salty and Spicy tie: the one with the lowest id wins. (Salty was created first = lowest id) */ assertEquals(5, profile.get(sweet.getId())); assertEquals(4, profile.get(bitter.getId())); assertEquals(3, profile.get(sour.getId())); assertEquals(2, profile.get(salty.getId())); assertEquals(1, profile.get(spicy.getId())); } The flavor tags are created in a fixed order, because ties are resolved on the lowest id, which makes the creation order part of the test’s preconditions. This test also verifies that the cascade from Spirit to its SpiritFlavorTag join entities works.
CocktailMenuDAOIntegrationTest: composite keys # CocktailMenu is mapped with @EmbeddedId and @MapsId, so its key is derived from two relations. The tests verify the following:
savedFavoriteCompositeKey():
A saved favorite can be found again with a CocktailMenuId, and @PrePersist has set savedAt. getFavoritesReturnsCocktails():
getFavoritesByUser() returns cocktails with their relations fetched (accessing getSpirit().getName() would throw without the JOIN FETCH chain). favoritesAreSeparatedPerUser():
Favorites are separated per user, so one user is never able to see another user’s favorites. deleteRemovesOnlyLink():
Deleting a favorite removes only the link, not the user or the cocktail. savingTheSameTwice():
Saving the same favorite twice is rejected by the composite primary key. The last test also explains a design choice in the service layer: CocktailMenuService.saveFavorite checks for duplicates before saving, so the user receives a clean 409 Conflict instead of a raw database error.
Mistakes along the way # Overall, the testing went smoothly. I only really encountered two problems, and both were reasonably easy to resolve:
Testcontainers version mismatch. My first configuration used the 1.x package and class names, but the project uses 2.x. The container class had moved packages and lost its generic type parameter, so the configuration had to be rewritten. @AfterAll instead of @AfterEach, as I described above. Known limitations # I want to be explicit about what these tests do not prove:
Database-level ON DELETE rules. Test tables are generated by Hibernate, not by schema.sql, so ON DELETE CASCADE and SET NULL do not exist in the test database. As mentioned, I chose not to write tests that delete a user and expect favorites to disappear, because they would fail for reasons unrelated to my code. Those rules are therefore not covered by any automatic test, and will be testest manually later after I have seeded my database with data from TheCocktailDB’s API.
getAll and the simple entities are not tested directly, since they use the same generic code as the tested paths. I expect that it will not be necessary to test all the other entities because of this, but of course I can never be completly sure that the code runs as it should without actually testing them. At the moment, however, I do not see the need for that.
QuizService as a whole. The pieces are covered (candidate filtering and profile calculation in the DAO tests, the distance function in the unit tests), but an end-to-end test of filtering, profile building and strategy working together is still outstanding. I chose to postpone it in favor of seeding real data first. However, I do need to write a QuizService test before I can confidently use the class’s methods.
REST-assured # REST-assured tests send real HTTP requests to running endpoints, so they can only be written once the Javalin layer exists. I have not built that layer yet, and therefore it will only be added later in the build process.
title: Entry 10 - Testing - Unit and Integration

content:
A central part of our third-semester API is to handle errors accurately and throw the corresponding exceptions. We have learned how important it is to log critical moments in the code, so that errors never go unnoticed.
A central exception class # At the moment, all my API’s business errors are thrown as ApiException, which carries a status code and a message and logs itself when it is created:
public class ApiException extends RuntimeException { private int code; private static final Logger logger = LoggerFactory.getLogger(ApiException.class); public ApiException(int code, String msg){ super(msg); this.code = code; logger.error("ApiException (code={}): {}", code, msg); } public ApiException (HttpStatus status, String msg) { this(status.getCode(), msg); } public int getCode(){ return code; } } Because the logging sits in the constructor itself, every throw new ApiException(...) is automatically logged in one central place, without the services having to log themselves.
Named status codes instead of magic numbers # I first wrote throw new ApiException(404, ...), but it is hard to remember what a number means. I considered writing my own enum, but chose to import Javalin’s io.javalin.http.HttpStatus, since the project is going to end up as a Javalin API and the enum is therefore already the right one. The extra constructor takes an HttpStatus, and getCode() still returns an int. The compiler now catches typos (CONFOLICT), which it never could with a bare number.
What should be logged? # I deliberately do not log cases where a field is simply null, for example when a cocktail has no liqueur. That is expected data, not an error, and logging it would drown out the real problems in noise. The log levels follow this rule of thumb:
ERROR: something failed that should not have (covered by ApiException and the transaction rollback in AbstractDAO) WARN: something unusual, but the app can continue INFO: important normal events (for example a new user created) DEBUG: detailed flow for troubleshooting I never log rawPassword or passwordHash, not even on errors. Passwords are sensitive data, and logging them could compromise the users’ security.
Where to go from here # Error and exception handling is a topic that will be in constant development throughout the API’s entire build process. Exceptions can happen in multiple places throughout the backend layers, and as the project grows, so does the risk of encountering one. Most of the Javalin and routing layer has not been built yet, and that is probably where most of the exception handling and logging will be.
I therefore expect this entry to grow considerably, with a lot more information and examples of correct exception handling.
UPDATED 16th October: Error handling in the seed: SeedException # In entries 11 and 12, I documented the whole seeding process of my database, with data fetched from TheCocktailDB API. That part of the process was complicated and demanding (which I also cover in detail there), and because the code can encounter exceptions in multiple places, I chose to capture these in their own SeedException class.
The importer could fail in a lot of different ways: it cannot read a CSV file, it cannot list raw/, the JSON cannot be parsed, or a drink cannot be saved. All of these throw a custom unchecked SeedException, which carries the original exception as its cause whenever it wraps another exception. At the moment, these exceptions are only logged manually in the classes that throw them. To optimize SeedException, the logging could be moved into the exception’s constructor, as I do in ApiException, so that every SeedException is logged in the same way.
Unchecked, because the caller cannot do anything sensible about a failed seed. If the file is missing, the right reaction is to stop and show the message, not to force every method up the call chain to declare throws. With a cause, so the original stack trace is not lost. The message says what I was doing (example: “Could not read classification files in database/seed”) and the cause says what actually went wrong. I made a seed-specific exception instead of reusing ApiException, because ApiException carries an HTTP status code and belongs to the REST layer. A failed import has nothing to do with HTTP, and therefore should not use an exception class dedicated to that.
title: Entry 9 - Error Handling and Logging

content:
The DAO layer is responsible for all communication with the database. I have made some of the project’s most important design decisions here.
Generic CRUD in one place # With 14 entities it would be wasteful to write create/read/update/delete 14 times. Instead, IDAO<T, ID> defines the contract and AbstractDAO<T, ID> implements it generically:
public interface IDAO <T, ID> { T create(T entity); Optional<T> getById(ID id); List<T> getAll(); T update(T entity); void delete(ID id); } There are two generic types because not all entities have the same kind of key. Most use Long, but join entities such as SpiritFlavorTag and CocktailMenu use their @EmbeddedId class. A concrete DAO therefore becomes very short:
public class SpiritDAO extends AbstractDAO<Spirit, Long> { public SpiritDAO(){ super(Spirit.class); } } Transactions and EntityManager handling # Each method opens its own EntityManager through try-with-resources, so it is always closed. All transaction logic is collected in one method, so begin/commit/rollback is not repeated:
protected T executeInTransaction(Function<EntityManager, T> action) { try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) { EntityTransaction emTransaction = em.getTransaction(); try { emTransaction.begin(); T result = action.apply(em); emTransaction.commit(); return result; } catch (RuntimeException e){ if (emTransaction.isActive()) { emTransaction.rollback(); } logger.error("Transaction failed, rolled back: {}", e.getMessage(), e); throw e; } } } Only write operations (create, update, delete) run in a transaction. Reading needs none. On error, the transaction is rolled back and the exception is logged before being rethrown.
Lazy loading and JOIN FETCH # This is the most central technical problem I encountered in the DAO layer. Because the relations are LAZY, and the EntityManager is closed when the DAO method returns, accessing a lazy relation afterwards throws a LazyInitializationException. I learned that this typically happens when a service maps an entity to a DTO.
There are a few ways to fix this problem. Two of them are obvious “root fixes” that I deliberately rejected:
Making everything EAGER. It does not remove the database calls, only their visibility, and it applies globally, even where the relations are not used. I learned that this is called the N+1 problem. If my database were small, this might not be such a serious problem. However, since I know that I will seed my database with over 600 cocktail recipes, and that each cocktail has six relations, fetching a simple list of all cocktails could trigger up to six extra queries per cocktail, even though I only need some of the information. Open Session in View (keeping the EntityManager open for the whole request). It hides when database calls happen and can hold connections open for unnecessarily long. It does not fix the N+1 problem, it only hides it. Of course, it will not generate any errors or exceptions, but it will make the site much slower. Another reason for not using this option is that it would compromise the separation of responsibilities between the layers that I described in Entry 3. With an open EntityManager, controllers and JSON mappers could trigger database calls, and data access would no longer be confined to the DAO layer. Instead, I use an explicit JOIN FETCH per use case (which is also the recommended practice), so each query fetches exactly what it needs and nothing more. This also means I avoid any LazyInitializationException. To avoid repetition, the join part is collected in one constant, while the WHERE part is deliberately different for each method:
public class CocktailDAO extends AbstractDAO<Cocktail, Long> { private static final String COCKTAIL_WITH_RELATIONS = "SELECT c FROM Cocktail c " + "LEFT JOIN FETCH c.cocktailFamily " + "LEFT JOIN FETCH c.spirit " + // LEFT JOIN FETCH because five of the six relations are nullable "LEFT JOIN FETCH c.liqueur " + "LEFT JOIN FETCH c.mixer " + "LEFT JOIN FETCH c.syrup " + "LEFT JOIN FETCH c.garnish "; public Optional<Cocktail> getByIdWithDetails(Long id) { try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) { String jpql = COCKTAIL_WITH_RELATIONS + "WHERE c.id = :id"; return em.createQuery(jpql, Cocktail.class) .setParameter("id", id) .getResultStream() .findFirst(); } } // Rest of class logic... } LEFT JOIN FETCH is used because the relations are nullable. A plain JOIN FETCH would exclude cocktails that are missing one of them, for example the Old Fashioned, which has no liqueur or mixer. All six relations are @ManyToOne (single values), so they can be joined at the same time without problems.
There is one important limitation to note: you cannot JOIN FETCH several List collections in the same query (it throws a MultipleBagFetchException). Therefore, the ingredients’ flavorTags lists are not fetched in the same query but are accessed while the EntityManager is still open (I will talk more about that in a later entry).
Specialized queries # Some user stories required more than simple CRUD methods. For example, login looks a user up by username. I chose this because username is the natural key. When a user logs in, the only things they enter are their username and password. The user does not know their id, because it is an auto-generated number (BIGSERIAL). They never see it and therefore cannot give it to the system. This requires username to be UNIQUE, so that the lookup matches at most one row.
public class UserDAO extends AbstractDAO<User, Long> { public UserDAO() { super(User.class); } public Optional<User> findByUsername(String username) { try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) { String jpql = "SELECT u FROM User u WHERE u.username = :username"; List<User> results = em.createQuery(jpql, User.class) .setParameter("username", username) .getResultList(); return results.stream().findFirst(); } } } Note that JPQL uses entity and field names (User, u.username), not table and column names (users, the username column). Hibernate translates to SQL through @Table/@Column, so a table can be renamed without touching queries.
Another example is “show my favorites”. In CocktailMenuDAO, the method getFavoritesByUser looks up by user id in a composite-key table and therefore needs a slightly more elaborate query.
title: Entry 6 - The DAO Layer

content:
The service layer contains the business logic and is the only layer that talks to both DAOs and DTOs.
Why DTOs? # Why do I even use DTOs when I could just use the entities I have already created? Well, that is because entities never leave the service layer, and there are three very important reasons for that:
Security. User contains passwordHash. If an entity is sent out directly (for example as JSON), the hash leaks to the frontend, which is less than ideal. A UserDTO simply does not have the field, so this issue cannot occur. Lazy loading. I have talked about lazy loading a lot at this point, and that is because it is probably the most annoying and most frequent problem I have encountered throughout the build process. DTOs are ideal for avoiding this problem because they are built from data that has already been fetched, so a LazyInitializationException cannot occur in a later layer. Control. With DTOs, I can deliberately choose what is exposed, and I can change the data model without changing how the API looks from the outside. I distinguish between response DTOs (what is sent out, for example CocktailDTO) and request DTOs (what is received, for example CreateCocktailDTO), since they have different fields and purposes. Lombok removes boilerplate, and mapping from an entity is done manually in a static factory method:
@Getter @AllArgsConstructor @NoArgsConstructor public class CocktailDTO { private Long id; private String name; private String description; private String instructions; private String cocktailFamily; private String spirit; private String liqueur; private String mixer; private String syrup; private String garnish; public static CocktailDTO fromEntity (Cocktail c) { return new CocktailDTO ( c.getId(), c.getName(), c.getDescription(), c.getInstructions(), c.getCocktailFamily() != null ? c.getCocktailFamily().getName() : null, c.getSpirit() != null ? c.getSpirit().getName() : null, c.getLiqueur() != null ? c.getLiqueur().getName() : null, c.getMixer() != null ? c.getMixer().getName() : null, c.getSyrup() != null ? c.getSyrup().getName() : null, c.getGarnish() != null ? c.getGarnish().getName() : null ); } } The null checks are necessary because the ingredients are optional. The DTO only contains the name of each relation, not the whole nested object, because the client only needs that much to display the recipe.
UserService and password security # Passwords are never stored in plain text. I use BCrypt, which is built for passwords: it is deliberately slow (making brute force impractical) and builds a unique random salt into every hash, so two identical passwords get different hashes. We have not covered the topic of security yet (we will be introduced to it later this week), so my approach to password security might change as development progresses. For now, however, I believe BCrypt works well for my API, though this decision is based on my very limited knowledge of security.
public class UserService { // Variables and constructor public UserDTO register(String username, String email, String rawPassword) { if (userDAO.findByUsername(username).isPresent()) { throw new ApiException(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "Username already in use: " + username); } String hashedPassword = BCrypt.hashpw(rawPassword, BCrypt.gensalt()); User savedUser = userDAO.create(new User(username, email, hashedPassword)); logger.info("New user created: {}", username); return UserDTO.fromEntity(savedUser); } public UserDTO login(String username, String rawPassword) { User user = userDAO.findByUsername(username) .orElseThrow(() -> new ApiException(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED, "Wrong username or password")); if (!BCrypt.checkpw(rawPassword, user.getPasswordHash())) { throw new ApiException(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED, "Wrong username or password"); // Same message no matter which of the two is wrong } return UserDTO.fromEntity(user); } // IsAdmin boolean method } The hash string contains the algorithm, the cost factor and the salt, which is why checkpw can recompute and compare without a separately stored salt. This is also why I never hash the entered password again and compare the two hashes with equals: the salts would be different. Login gives the same error message whether the username does not exist or the password is wrong, so an attacker cannot tell which usernames exist.
CocktailMenuService: existence checks and duplicates # The save-favorite logic validates before it writes. It checks that the link does not already exist (409, HttpStatus.CONFLICT) and that both the user and the cocktail exist (404, HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND). This gives clear errors instead of cryptic database errors.
public class CocktailMenuService { // Variables public CocktailDTO saveFavorite (Long userId, Long cocktailId) { CocktailMenuId id = new CocktailMenuId(userId, cocktailId); if (cocktailMenuDAO.getById(id).isPresent()) { throw new ApiException(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "The cocktail is already saved as a favorite"); } User user = userDAO.getById(userId) .orElseThrow(() -> new ApiException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "User does not exist: " + userId)); Cocktail cocktail = cocktailDAO.getByIdWithDetails(cocktailId) .orElseThrow(() -> new ApiException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Cocktail does not exist: " + cocktailId)); cocktailMenuDAO.create(new CocktailMenu(user, cocktail)); return CocktailDTO.fromEntity(cocktail); } // Get and remove methods } The full User and Cocktail objects are fetched for two reasons. The lookups double as the existence checks, and the CocktailMenu entity needs real entity references: its user and cocktail fields are annotated with @MapsId (just like the SpiritFlavorTag example in Entry 5), so Hibernate derives the composite key from them when the row is saved.
CocktailService: validation and role check # The business rules that I deliberately kept out of the database live here:
public class CocktailService { // Variables, constructor, getById() and getAll() methods // Admin method - for admin to create new cocktail in database public CocktailDTO createCocktail(CreateCocktailDTO request, UserDTO admin) { if (!userService.isAdmin(admin)) { throw new ApiException(HttpStatus.FORBIDDEN, "Only admins can create new cocktails"); } if (request.getSpiritId() == null && request.getLiqueurId() == null && request.getMixerId() == null && request.getSyrupId() == null) { throw new ApiException(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "A cocktail must have at least one ingredient (spirit, liqueur, mixer or syrup)"); } // ... looks up the family and the chosen ingredients, then creates and saves the cocktail } } The role check reuses userService.isAdmin(...), so the rule for “what is an admin” exists in one place. The service takes a UserDTO and does not look up the user itself. It relies on the caller (the upcoming Javalin layer) having already determined who is logged in.
title: Entry 7 - DTOs and the Service Layer

content:
This is the application’s most complex and academically interesting part: how the user’s answers become a recommended recipe. A large part of the application’s core logic and purpose lives here, and it will be the heart of the finished product once both the backend and the frontend are complete.
I expect this layer to evolve and change a lot throughout the build process, especially if there is time for some of the “nice-to-have” user stories.
Overview of the flow # At the moment, within my current scope, this is what the quiz flow looks like:
Drink family is a hard filter: only cocktails in the chosen family are considered. The filtering happens in the database. Spirit is an optional hard filter: if the user picks a spirit, the candidates are filtered on it. If they pick none (null), all spirits pass through. Taste: the user gives a score from 1 to 5 for each of the five flavor dimensions (Sweet, Sour, Bitter, Salty, Spicy). The candidates are scored against the user’s answers, and the one with the smallest distance wins. Candidates and filtering # Both the filters and the candidate selection happen in a single DAO call. The spirit filter is only added if the user has chosen a spirit, which is why the query is built with a StringBuilder. A String is immutable, so every + creates a new copy, while a StringBuilder is modified in place. I could have solved this in another way, but the real advantage of StringBuilder here is that the query is built up step by step, depending on a condition:
public class CocktailDAO extends AbstractDAO<Cocktail, Long> { // Variable, constructor, getByIdWithDetails() and getAllWithDetails() methods public List<CocktailCandidate> getCandidatesForQuiz(Long familyId, Long spiritId) { try (EntityManager em = emf.createEntityManager()) { StringBuilder jpql = new StringBuilder(COCKTAIL_WITH_RELATIONS) // StringBuilder because there is a conditional structure .append("WHERE c.cocktailFamily.id = :familyId"); if (spiritId != null) { jpql.append(" AND c.spirit.id = :spiritId"); // Conditional = only append if user chooses a spirit type } var query = em.createQuery(jpql.toString(), Cocktail.class) .setParameter("familyId", familyId); if (spiritId != null) { query.setParameter("spiritId", spiritId); } List<Cocktail> cocktails = query.getResultList(); List<CocktailCandidate> candidates = new ArrayList<>(); for (Cocktail cocktail : cocktails) { candidates.add(new CocktailCandidate (cocktail, buildFlavorProfile(cocktail))); } return candidates; } } // buildFlavorProfile() and rankFlavorProfile() methods } buildFlavorProfile runs inside the same try block, while the EntityManager is still open. The query above fetches each cocktail’s spirit, liqueur, mixer and syrup, but each of those has a flavorTags list that is LAZY and therefore not loaded yet. buildFlavorProfile needs exactly those lists to add up the intensities, and the first time one of them is accessed, Hibernate sends an extra query to fetch it. That only works while the EntityManager is open. Had I called the method from the service layer instead, it would have thrown a LazyInitializationException.
The obvious solution would be to JOIN FETCH the lists in the same query, like the other relations, but Hibernate does not allow fetching several List collections at once (MultipleBagFetchException). Instead, the lists are loaded one at a time through lazy loading, which means one small extra query per ingredient.
This is the N+1 pattern I rejected in Entry 6, but here it is a deliberate trade-off. The query is already filtered by family, and possibly by spirit, so it only covers a small subset of the cocktails. Hibernate also reuses the same object within one EntityManager, so if ten cocktails use gin, its flavor tags are only fetched once - the number of extra queries follows the number of distinct ingredients, not the number of cocktails. And unlike EAGER, which would trigger extra queries everywhere a cocktail is read, this happens in one place, in one method, where it is visible in the code.
A cocktail’s flavor profile # A cocktail’s profile is calculated from its ingredients in two steps. First, the intensity per flavor dimension is summed across all ingredients:
private Map<Long, Integer> buildFlavorProfile(Cocktail cocktail) { Map <Long, Integer> sums = new HashMap<>(); if (cocktail.getSpirit() != null) { for (SpiritFlavorTag tag : cocktail.getSpirit().getFlavorTags()) { sums.merge(tag.getFlavorTag().getId(), tag.getIntensity(), Integer::sum); } } // likewise for liqueur, mixer and syrup return rankFlavorProfile(sums); } Map.merge(key, value, Integer::sum) inserts the value if the key is new, and otherwise adds it to the existing one. I chose sum over average or maximum because a strong sour ingredient could otherwise be diluted away (average) or hide all the other ingredients (maximum). With the sum, I get a truer picture of a cocktail’s flavor profile, because it reflects how much each dimension takes up in the drink overall.
Next, the dimensions are ranked by sum and given the scores 5, 4, 3, 2, 1:
private Map<Long, Integer> rankFlavorProfile(Map<Long, Integer> sums){ if (sums.isEmpty()) { return sums; } List<Map.Entry<Long, Integer>> sortedEntries = new ArrayList<>(sums.entrySet()); sortedEntries.sort((a, b) -> { int compareBySum = b.getValue() - a.getValue(); // Highest sum first if(compareBySum != 0) { return compareBySum; } return a.getKey().compareTo(b.getKey()); // deterministic - if two sums are equal }); Map<Long, Integer> ranked = new HashMap<>(); int score = sortedEntries.size(); for (Map.Entry<Long, Integer> entry : sortedEntries) { ranked.put(entry.getKey(), score); score--; } return ranked; } A worked example:
Three ingredients give the sums: Sweet 14, Bitter 10, Sour 9, Salty 8 and Spicy 4. After ranking, the profile becomes: Sweet 5, Bitter 4, Sour 3, Salty 2, Spicy 1. Keeping all five dimensions (rather than only the dominant one) means the distance to the user’s answers can be calculated meaningfully. Ties are resolved by flavorTagId, because a HashMap otherwise gives no guaranteed order and the result could vary between runs.
The Strategy pattern for matching # So now I have all these methods to help compare the cocktails’ profiles to the user’s answers, but none of them actually does the comparing. That is because the comparison itself is isolated behind an interface in the app/strategies package:
public interface ScoringStrategy { double calculateDistance(Map<Long, Integer> userAnswers, Map<Long, Integer> cocktailProfile); } public class EuclideanDistanceStrategy implements ScoringStrategy { @Override public double calculateDistance(Map<Long, Integer> userAnswers, Map<Long, Integer> cocktailProfile) { Set<Long> allFlavorTagIds = new HashSet<>(); allFlavorTagIds.addAll(userAnswers.keySet()); allFlavorTagIds.addAll(cocktailProfile.keySet()); double sumOfSquares = 0; for (Long tagId : allFlavorTagIds){ int userValue = userAnswers.getOrDefault(tagId, 0); int cocktailValue = cocktailProfile.getOrDefault(tagId, 0); int difference = userValue - cocktailValue; sumOfSquares += (double) difference * difference; } return Math.sqrt(sumOfSquares); } } Euclidean distance is the Pythagorean theorem generalized to more dimensions (here five): the square root of the sum of the squared differences. This means that a shorter distance is a better match, and 0 is a perfect match.
An example:
The user answers is: Sweet 5, Sour 1, Bitter 1, Salty 1, Spicy 1. The cocktail has the profile: Sweet 5, Sour 3, Bitter 4, Salty 2, Spicy 1. The differences are: 0, 2, 3, 1, 0 So the distance is: √(0+4+9+1+0) = √14 ≈ 3.74. It is important to note that a cocktail always has all five flavor dimensions, because its ingredients together cover every flavor tag in my seed data. The ranking therefore always gives the scores 5 to 1. cocktailProfile.getOrDefault(tagId, 0) is only a safety net in case a dimension should ever be missing.
The point of the Strategy pattern is that QuizService only knows the interface. The strategy is injected from outside, so the algorithm can be swapped, if ever needed, without changing the service:
public class QuizService { private final CocktailDAO cocktailDAO; private final ScoringStrategy scoringStrategy; public QuizService (ScoringStrategy scoringStrategy) { this.cocktailDAO = new CocktailDAO(); this.scoringStrategy = scoringStrategy; } public CocktailDTO findBestMatch (QuizAnswerDTO answers) { List<CocktailCandidate> candidates = cocktailDAO.getCandidatesForQuiz( answers.getCocktailFamilyId(), answers.getSpiritId()); if (candidates.isEmpty()) { throw new ApiException(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "No recipes match the chosen cocktail family/spirit type"); } CocktailCandidate bestMatch = null; double bestDistance = Double.MAX_VALUE; for (CocktailCandidate candidate : candidates) { double distance = scoringStrategy.calculateDistance( answers.getTasteAnswers(), candidate.getFlavorProfile()); if (distance < bestDistance) { bestDistance = distance; bestMatch = candidate; } } return CocktailDTO.fromEntity(bestMatch.getCocktail()); } } The instantiation happens in one place: new QuizService(new EuclideanDistanceStrategy()).

content:
Database # One of the first things I dug into was the relationships between the entities in my domain model, and how they would map to the tables in my database. The database has changed quite a bit from my original thinking when I drew up my first domain model. This is due to a number of challenges I ran into, and an even larger number of important decisions. This took my idea from a simple hand-drawn domain model to a detailed and well-thought-out database structure that satisfies 1NF, 2NF and 3NF.
At the moment, my ERD diagram looks like this:
Important decisions and reasoning # Schema # I decided to build my schema.sql and database first before my Java entities. This means that the entities mirror the tables, and not the other way around. schema.sql is therefore “the truth”, not Hibernate’s auto-generated guesses. All though it can come in handy somethimes that Hibernate can generate tables automatically (hbm2ddl.auto=create) - it can also has its down sides like how its guesses about column types and constraints are imprecise. With a hand-written schema I control data types, CHECK constraints and foreign keys myself, and I can prove that the entities and the schema agree
The script lives in database/ in the project root and not in src/main/resources. It is run manually against PostgreSQL and is not part of the application’s runtime, so it should not be packaged into the JAR.
Flavor profiles: join tables with intensity # As I mentioned in the post about my idea, the user should be able to choose a cocktail based on a flavor preference. This is the most important aspect of my API - you could even go as far as to say it is part of the main purpose.
Every ingredient (Spirit, Liqueur, Mixer, Syrup) has an intensity from 1 to 5 for each flavor dimension (sweet, sour, bitter, salty, spicy). These flavor profiles are modeled as FlavorTag + join tables holding an intensity value for each ingredient type, such as spirit_flavor_tag. Since an ordinary @ManyToMany relationship cannot hold extra columns, the join tables have to be entities of their own with composite keys.
CREATE TABLE flavor_tag ( id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE ); CREATE TABLE spirit_flavor_tag ( spirit_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES spirit(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, flavor_tag_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES flavor_tag(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, intensity SMALLINT NOT NULL CHECK (intensity BETWEEN 1 AND 5), PRIMARY KEY (spirit_id, flavor_tag_id) ); The primary key is composed of the two foreign keys, so an ingredient can only have one intensity per flavor dimension. The CHECK constraint guarantees at the database level that the intensity is between 1 and 5, so invalid data can never get in, regardless of which code writes to the table.
CocktailMenu join table # CocktailMenu was chosen to be a join table between User and Cocktail called user_favorite_cocktail. Its main purpose is to hold the users’ saved favorites, and also has an extra column, saved_at. This table covers a big part of user story 2.
CREATE TABLE user_favorite_cocktail ( user_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, cocktail_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES cocktail(id) ON DELETE CASCADE, saved_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now(), PRIMARY KEY (user_id, cocktail_id) ); The main table cocktail - what defines it? # When I was building the tables and their relationships to each other, I asked myself an important question: “What does a cocktail actually contain in my system?”
My first draft made Spirit, Liqueur, Mixer and Syrup required on a cocktail. That did not hold up in reality: Cocktails such as the Old Fashioned only have a base alcohol (Spirit) and ice, so all the other category columns would end up being NULL. My thought was then to make Liqueur, Mixer, Syrup and Garnish nullable and keep only Spirit as NOT NULL, but that was not possible either, since some recipes are non-alcoholic.
So in the end, only cocktail_family_id is NOT NULL among the relationships, and all the others are nullable:
CREATE TABLE cocktail ( id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE, description TEXT, instructions TEXT NOT NULL, cocktail_family_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES cocktail_family(id) ON DELETE RESTRICT, spirit_id BIGINT REFERENCES spirit(id) ON DELETE SET NULL, liqueur_id BIGINT REFERENCES liqueur(id) ON DELETE SET NULL, mixer_id BIGINT REFERENCES mixer(id) ON DELETE SET NULL, syrup_id BIGINT REFERENCES syrup(id) ON DELETE SET NULL, garnish_id BIGINT REFERENCES garnish(id) ON DELETE SET NULL, created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL DEFAULT now() ); The rule “a cocktail must have at least one ingredient” is a business rule and is therefore enforced in the service layer, not as a database constraint. This keeps the schema flexible and puts the logic where it can be tested and produce a meaningful error message.
Non-alcoholic drinks are modeled as a cocktail_family (“Mocktails”) rather than a separate is_alcoholic flag. This is simpler and fits naturally with the quiz’s first question about drink family.
Foreign key strategy # The choice of ON DELETE behavior is deliberate and follows how “heavy” the relationship is:
RESTRICT on cocktail_family: a family that is used by cocktails cannot be deleted by accident. SET NULL on ingredients and garnish: if an ingredient is deleted, the cocktail simply loses that ingredient, which is possible because the columns are nullable. CASCADE on favorites and flavor tags: they are dependent links that make no sense without their parent. Data from TheCocktailDB # The database is seeded once from TheCocktailDB, instead of the application making constant live calls to the API.
The reasoning is that the API does not contain flavor profiles, which, as I mentioned, are the core data of my system. The flavor profiles are necessary for the user to be able to filter the recipes by flavor.
In addition, the ingredients are just unstructured strings that would have to be normalized in my database anyway, and my admin user story (9) requires that my own database is the source of truth. That is the user story that lets an Admin add new recipes to the database.
